title: Skip check: can you leave this section?

what.md: This section was not about a definition — the definition of a hypergraph was settled in Chapter 1. It was about **provenance**: where the groups in your data come from, and what the answer changes. If you can do all five of the following unaided, skip ahead.

items: Say which restriction a hypergraph relaxes, and name two structures that relax other restrictions instead.
State the two equivalent definitions of a hypergraph and translate one column of an incidence matrix back into a set.
Say whether a given dataset's hyperedges are native or constructed, and what follows from the answer.
Name two procedures for constructing hyperedges when the data has none, and say what parameter each introduces.
Explain why keeping a hypergraph intact is a substantive choice rather than a stylistic one.

what.md: The bar is unaided recall on all five. The fourth one is the one that carries a chapter of consequences — if you hesitate there, stay for cards 4 and 5, because Chapter 7's critique of the untested $k$ is written directly on top of them.

quiz.q: Which pair of structures relaxes *different* restrictions from a hypergraph?

opts.expl: Both relax restrictions on edges between an existing pair, and both still require exactly two endpoints. They sit alongside the hypergraph rather than covering its ground.

Correct: direction and kinds are independent axes from arity. This is why the paper's citation and follow datasets involve a *different* simplification — treating directed relations as undirected — that has nothing to do with the hypergraph machinery.
Those are two ways of writing a structure down, not structures in their own right. Both can describe a graph or a hypergraph.

quiz.q: A dataset of 600 users and their 2,000 shopping sessions has sessions of 7 items on average. How many memberships does the item-side hypergraph contain?
quiz.hint: Sessions × average basket size. The user count is a distractor.
quiz.sol: $2{,}000 \times 7 = 14{,}000$ memberships. The 600 users are irrelevant to this count — they do not appear in the item hypergraph at all. Noticing that an irrelevant number has been supplied is a habit worth building; problems rarely announce their distractors.

quiz.q: Two papers report results on the same named dataset, but one builds its hyperedges by $k$-NN with $k = 5$ and the other by co-authorship. Their numbers differ substantially. What has happened?

opts.md: One of them made an error
opts.expl: Not necessarily — and assuming an error is the least useful of the available conclusions. Both constructions are defensible, and both produce a real hypergraph over the same underlying records.

opts.md: They are reporting on functionally different objects that share a name, so the numbers are not directly comparable
opts.expl: Correct. A dataset name identifies the records, not the structure built from them. This is a common and quiet source of apparent disagreement in the literature, and it is why the method section matters as much as the results table.

opts.md: The dataset must have been updated between the two papers
opts.expl: Possible in general, but it is a specific claim that needs evidence. The construction difference is visible in the two methods sections and accounts for the discrepancy without any such assumption.

quiz.q: Why does the choice to keep a hypergraph intact rather than expand it matter beyond computational cost?

opts.md: Because expansion cannot represent weighted relations
opts.expl: Weights survive expansion perfectly well — you can weight a clique's edges. The problem is representation of *groups*, not of magnitudes.

opts.md: Because every expansion destroys the fact that certain relations constituted one event, and no downstream method can recover it
opts.expl: Correct. The information is gone at expansion time. This is the strongest argument for this paper's design stance, and it is worth crediting as a genuine strength when Chapter 7 turns to criticism.

opts.md: Because expanded graphs are always denser than the machine can store
opts.expl: Density is a real problem at scale — 481,671 edges from one hyperedge — but it is a practical limit, not the conceptual one. Star expansion stays linear and still loses the grouping.

close: **Section complete.** The next card is paper-specific: how *this* paper uses hypergraphs — the incidence matrix in its notation, the ten datasets, and the counting equation that opens Chapter 5.
